description: We are a mix of college students and new grads who are looking to expand our knowledge about space exploration
summary:
We built Lunar Landing Site Navigator - a web app showing when the Sun and Earth are visible from any spot on the Moon, for the nine Artemis III regions or custom coordinates, 2026 to 2035.

How it works?
1. We use NASA’s SPICE ephemeris plus LOLA elevation maps - near the south pole the Sun or Earth only counts once it clears the skyline
2. We land within 2.0 percentage points of NASA’s own sunlight maps, a smooth Moon is off by 19.7

What you get?
1. A 3D Moon globe and timeline of sunlight, Earth visibility, and when both overlap
2. Longest dark stretch and longest comm blackout for any stay
3. Rank all nine regions for a landing date, or find a site’s best dates in any year

How we ranked landing sites?
1. Flatness - at least 95% of a 100 m landing zone has to be under 10° slope
2. Nearby high ground - a walkable panel spot within 200 m, under 20° slope, on a 10 m mast
3. Tonnage - crew size and stay length stay fixed, so air, food and water are the same everywhere. Only the solar panels and battery change, so we rank by that weight, based on how much sunlight there is and how consistent it is

Why it matters?
Ranking by weight instead of average sunlight saves mass in 8 of 9 regions, up to 9.3 t
power and comms decide if a crew survives, so this makes the trade-offs easy to see
details:
What it does

  • Pick one of the nine Artemis III regions or enter custom coordinates, then pick a date range.
  • It shows a 3D Moon globe, a timeline of when it’s sunlit, when Earth is in view and when both overlap, plus metrics like longest dark stretch and longest comm blackout.
  • It ranks the nine regions for a landing date, finds a site’s best landing dates for any year 2026-2035, and compares up to four stays side by side.
  • “Where to land?” gives each region’s safe landing targets, where the panels go, and the solar array plus battery a year-round crewed base has to bring.
  • There’s also an AI chat that answers questions about all of it. The numbers it reports come from our own code, not the model.

How it works

  • SPICE kernels tell us where the Sun, Earth and Moon are, and LOLA elevation maps give each site a real skyline near the south pole.
  • The Sun or Earth only counts as up when it clears that skyline.
  • Targets are ranked by flatness, nearby high ground and kit weight (see above).

Benefits and impact

  • Planners can see which site and date give the best light and Earth contact.
  • Ranking by weight instead of average sunlight saves mass in 8 of 9 regions, up to 9.3 t.
  • The goal is to help pick landing sites where a crew can keep power and comms with the least mass to launch.

Tools

  • Python, skyfield, numpy, FastAPI, rasterio and pyproj for the engine and API.
  • Vite, Three.js and D3 for the frontend.
  • Cloudflare Pages, Workers AI and Containers for hosting and chat, with Cloud Run and Firebase as fallback.
  • Claude helped write much of the code, and we directed, reviewed and tested it.

What’s creative

  • We rank by tonnage to orbit, not just average sunlight. A site with steadier power needs less battery and fewer panels. That saves mass in 8 of 9 regions, by up to 9.3 tons.
  • You can also stand on the surface at any site and walk around as if you were there, with a realistic horizon and terrain shadows. Shadowed ground looks close to pitch black, as it really does. From there you can spot the best solar panel location and walk right up to it.

What we considered

  • Crew size and stay length are fixed, so air, food and water cost the same everywhere and are left out.
  • Panels are within 300 m of touchdown and on a 10 m mast, with walkable paths under 20°
  • The 20 m map has limits, like missing craters smaller than a pixel, and targets are pre-shortlisted by NASA’s sunlight map.
